GMCPOInDeIt EXT.:ISIOn on G0LA...111..—.412 explosion! of gunpowder occurred at Golborne, on Saturday. Injuries oft mom nature resulted to a collier named Rolgrt Jones, and his wife, and two other members of the family had a narrow escape. Jones is in the employ of Messrs. B. Evans and Coat Edge-green Colliery, and resides at Windy Bank. Ina cottagebelonging to the company. Jones was engaged In unpacking sonar grocery goads, amongst which was a parcel containing six pounds of blasting powder. He had hr pipe in his niouth and some ash from the tobacco falling on the powder, an explosion occurred, blowing out the door of the kitchen and smashing the panes of glass in the win- dows. Jones's clothes were set on fire and he ran out into the lane. The neighbour+ speedily put out the dames, hut not until the unfortunate man was badly burned about the heed. neck, fare, and hand, kir,. Jones was also severely , burned, and both she and her hu,band have aince been ' removed to the Wigan Iminnary. Flee injuies from which they are suffering are of a most wrious clmracter, but are not expected to terminate fatally in either case. A child was lying in a cradle in the kitchen but happily emtped unhurt, as did an elder son of the family, who war upstairs at the time, although the plaster of the room was shaken from the walls and other &image done to the house and furniture. There are tine children, and it is fortunate that they were out of the home at the time of the accident. _

BIGOTRY has once more scored a victory lathe House of Ginnie., tut its triumph will be short-lived, and the siquence will be the removal of the remaining fetters which check the fall advent of civil and religious freedom. I believe the general feeling in the town of Runcorn in regard to the conviction of Mr. Joseph William., gentleman, for tampering with a voting paper at the recent election of guardian., is one of regret and astonishment. Many people in the town have for wine weeks been inclined to think that when the charge was repeatedly adjournvd, in order that further snatch might he made for the missing witnesa, Halstead, it was pushing the matter a little too far, and causing unneceseary pain to a noon who was in high esteem amongst many of the rate- payers. However, the Bench seems to have been able In look much further ahead than those who differed in opinion and even the attempt of counsel (Mr. Seger) did not oppose to have the slightest influence in shaking • determination to not allow any legal quibble to prevent the law taking its course. We all know that in ths fierce com- petition for place which occurs at an election time, in toy questionalda tricks are often resorted to by friends on each side whom zeal often outruns their diecretion. and who seem to have for their motto some similar saying to that of 'All is fair in love and war." For some years past it has been broadly hinted Icy thnee who professed to he better posted than their fellows, that the manner in which the voting papers were tilled up at the election of Guardians for the township of Runcorn was far from being above sus- picion, but no action appears to have been taken with the object of sifting the truth of these statements until the data of the last cmtest. It is to be hoped that the heavy line inflicted upon Mr. Williams, and the serious costs to which he ninst have been put in defending the Iction will cocoa different effect upon any other men who are food of meddling in town's matter, and keep them front trying any moves of a goes- lion:obit, character at such contests. The result of tke trial canna havd raised Mr. Williams in the estinmtion of the pelif ic. aml what swill be his feelings when he again t .kes his seat at the Board-room table I cannot profess Cocoon hint abbot tiny concoct, in the nature of things, be of amen phosumbh, char,rter. Tbereare gentlemen in the town who bate uot ser upl,ll to ray that the prosecution was the result of private pique on the part of • ceatalit gentleman: think that thoos who have any personal knowledge whatever of the respicted clerk to the Guardians , will agree with me in the belief that lie would not have lent himself, for one moment, to the carrying out of any scheme for the gratification of each a feeling on the port of env one. Mr. Linaker, as the returning officer appointed by the Board of Guardians, has certain public duties to perform, and how he could possibly have neglected to report the state of the papers which had been tampered with to the Galardi:ma, and at the xime time acted in a manner becoming an official placed in his position. I arn at a loon to determine. Others interested in the case talk as if the assistant overseer (Mr. Sutton,) h.I taken mine independent action in the prolecit- tion, but these are app orently entirely ObliVlolls of the fact that during an election of Guardians. that official is bound toy law to sot under the control of the returning officer.

Lord Juse.ce James said that if a lean, therefore, told a lit in an inferior court, and was prosecuted and sentenced in respect of it, he would not then be punishable for telling the tutor lie afterwards in a superior cou..t. ' .

Mr. Jones said that, honing tree punished for the offence, he had purged himself from it. and could not Ise again tried for the same proceeding But if he were to perjure himself in another proceeding he I.ohl be committing anew offence. Because a man. frotn the exigencies of our tu lto.al eystem, committed a number of perjuries, it would be monstrous to take them one by one and punish him for each. Lord JusticeJarnes asked what was the proposition of law which it was sought to prove. Mr. Jones replied that his point was that they might join any nomher of counts in an indictment for misde- meanour bemuse the decision thereon was only ono judgment. Mr. Justice Bramwell observed that there was some mi. apprehension as to the meaning of" one judgment." ltdid not mean that there was to be only one sentence, but that the judgment on each count was the same. Mr. Janes Said that he based his argument on the principle that in misdemeanour, as opposed to felony counts for seve- ral nsisdemeanours might be joinvth beMuse the verdict passed would be " guilty " or "not guilty " of misdemea- nour. Then, with regard to the statutes, he contended that there was no power to inflict penal servitude without a com- mon law punishment, aml, further, he urged that the nomad term of seven years was utterly void Lord Jusfice James asked if the learned counsel wished the court to review the whole sentence, and consider the desirability of increasing it, as it had power to do on a writ frr°'
!Nei-Jones said he did not wish that, but he wai. there to , ask that justice should be done.

On the conclusion of the learned counsel's argument, the Attorney-general (Sir Henry James) said he did not know whether be should he justified in occupying the public time, but he might tell their lordships that there was an answer to every opposition brought forward by the other side founded on authority. Mr. Benjamin, QC, then replied tor the error, and the Attorney-General also spoke on the ease. Lord Justice James gate judgment. holding that the writ of error had been imprudently granted by the late Attorney- I general, and that the two sentences of term o years' penal eerritude had been eighth indicted for two offences of per- jure, althenigh eommittad in furtherance of a fraud to obtain soother person's estates. Lords Judea, Bramwell ant Brett concurred, and judg- meot was therefore given for the Crown. The result is that the Cltimant will remain in penal servi.' tode for another seven yeus after his first term unites he receive. a free pardon.

StrOoXIXO Snaps or Sr. Hubiews.—A very shocking case of suicide occurred on Wedresday night, in Campbell- street, Eccleston. It appears that the mart, Richard Brigge, was an earthenware dealer, and 37 years of age, and had been noticed to be in low spirits for the past few weeks. On one occasion he remarked that if he had wale poison he would put amend Co his existence, and subsequent events have transpired which showed he was in earnest. About half-past ten on Wednesday morning his wife saw him drinking at the Church Tavern, Westfield-street, and asked Iron to assist her in hawking some pots. He told her logo and he would follow immediately, and she left, but saw nothing of him until she stw him In the bedroom, hanging op the neck with a cord, at bolt-past eleven the same eight. ! DEATH UNIoER PECULIAR CIRCUMSTANCES. An inquest nor held on Tueslay afternoon at the Cattage Hospital before Mr. Driflield, coroner, on the body of Peter Crab:man, met with his death under the circumstances I detailed below o—NlArtin liahagan, AT, tirant.street, Sr. Helens, a miner unable to work through injuries receivq, mid that deceased was his father, and was 112 years of age. He worked at Pilkington's colliery, where he loot worked, at different times, ab,ut 18 years. Ile lodged at Oroves-row, and witness SAW him well last ,olicout a month ago. Witnem Clone on Wednesday evening to the Cottage Hospital to see his father, who was then in a bad condition, and was rambling. Deceased told witness that when engaged Cl work one wagon knocked against another, and he wan knocked down by a bar with which he was "prising," and ! lon fell on his back.—Mary Ellen Bates, wife of Joe. Bates,: 62, Bock Grove-street, deposed that deceased lodged with her nearly three yeam, and won working at the Colliery all the time. On Friday, the Ilth, he went to his work in the morning as motel, and appealed to he all right. Ile came home between hour and live o'clock in the evening—lois usual tioneatoot complained of being ill as mon as he entered the house. He remarked that he was never no bad in hi. life. Witness urged hion to take a cup of t 0.., which Be dratok, but I 11.1 not hing within. He went to bed in about a quarter of : an hour, null complaining of being unwell. In the night deceased said that the pain was in the small of his back, mol witness then applied bran poultices to the parts complained of. Ile asked for nothing beta cup of tea. Ile WOrnOt sick. Next day he woe still in pain, and his bowels were purged a little, the matter being chiefly blood—ln answer to the coroner, witness said that a doctor would not come without • note from the colliery. This was obtained by a party who knew the decemeol, and the doctor arrived on the Sunday following. The doctor'e instructions were in apply 0 br.ou poultice, and keep lon. and she obeyed the instructions. On Tuesday morning he W. very bad, and ap- peared to he losing hie senses. On the same morning Inn no, removed in o cart to the Hospital. Decease(' did not coy wiaat MOS itoe cause lilt itnose. He had never been no itl before to the oitno se's knowledge. Witness went to the hospital on Saturday, and was present when Ile died.—Francie Hay, physician and surgeon with Dr. (taskell. mid that he heard of the case on Saturday wed., the 12.11, from his amistant, Mr Knowles, who visited hint on Sunday. The person who brought the inforniation gave the wrong aohlrem, and therefore be mulol not see the d aeceril, though he tried on Saturday. The report which Ike assistant male was not that the cane woe serious, but that the deceased had pain, in floe back. lie (witness) was tohl that floe demons' come personally to the surgery on Monday for • note to go to the hospital. (The caroler ap- peared surprimd at this statement.) He (witness) on Tues- day fouled the deceased in Ind at the beepital, where Ile was being alterded to. He complained of a slight tenderness over the tower part el the back, but the thief matter wane eevere cough and congestion of the lungs, from which the cough arose. On Thursday decemed expressed himself as ranch better. Witnem did not eve him on Friday. Ha diod on Satunlay at about two o'clock. Witnehe bawd that de- ceased was wrong in Inc bowels, but deceased did not com- plain of this to witness,and neveriaveanv particulars onto the accident which bekt hitt,. IS nom Sad made a poet- mortem examination of the deceased that day, and the ...Ise of death was con,gestion of the homes sumrveninepn ' old sanding disease of the heart and lungs. The heart was !enlarged with a deposit from tlov bowels, and the texture of the heart itself was soft and fatty. l'he longs were oleaginous. The deceased looked older than the age given by hie friends. There was a little redness over, the breast bone, but there were no particular marks of either external or internal injury. There was a slight patch of congestion of the bladder, but that wee not the result of any accident. It would account for the red character of the urine. lie found nothing which was likely to have accelerated doolb. By a Juror TLe congestion 00 110.. lungs would not have been brought on loy any injury.—Mayy Ann Bates, being re-calletL the Coroner elicited-Dail her float tie CeaSed went to the surgery himself for a note for the Loaf:dial. The Coroder said the was the worst thinJ that could have happened.—Bartholo- mew Conlon an old man residing in tenon'',Pow, and • Maurer at the colliery, said that he asked the deimsed brow Ire got hurt, and he replied, "With shifthog some wagons o the bar caught me on the front and I fell upon my back." Deceased worked some time after, nod he was working when be made the above statement to witnees. That night de- ceased seemed very poorly, and on the next d y witness oh- Mined a note from Mr. France, the manager of the collieries. —The Coroner mid that the ninth.] evidence show,' only natural causem though they were told that oboe struck de- mised on the chest or on 0100 belly. SAD DROWNING CASK—GALLANT CONDUCT. An inquest RAS held on Tuesday:at the Black Horse inn, before Mr. Dritlisld, on the body of Peter Brornilow, oho met with his death by drowning on Monday night in the :eanni near the rallway.—James Brondlow, 121, Park-road, collier, said: The deceased was my son, and was 25 years 'f age. lie worked eta collier at Glover's colliery.' in Sal- on.' I heard abr. Ms death It on e sarne evenlini: I lead ' him brought from his lodgings in Rimmer-street, behind the baths. I believe ha had no mark of hurt, and to have been bathing when he wee drowned. I never heard him talk about srtimnfing, and don't know whether he could swim or not. He has not worked any since last Thursday.— Richard .I..immti, 21, Parr-street, said: The deceased lalced to or ate in Rimmosatreet. Yestsrslay afternoon I met with decease!. and we made it up to go to the canal and haven twins We were both swimmers, I believe. We were by ourselves. As we room walking along the road 1 said to him "Can you swim P' and he replied a Yes." 1 Ramo away from him, and in a short time I heard a shout, rs He's drowning." I came back, but he was out of sight then. I dive lion bins twice, hut could not find him. I swam away to get out, and on reaching the bank the folks helped me out. Whilst 1 was ilreming I heard that he had beeo got out. We had both lied drink, but In W. not more intoxicated thin I was Ile did not say he intended to do anything to himself.—Edward Littler, Sutton Moss, a collier, said I was passing over the canal Midge at about sine o'clock on Monday night. People said there waa a swim- ming match on, and Iran to the place where a man was coming out of the canal. I told John Quinn, who is a ewimmer, to strip and go in and rescue the drowning man. He went ie. and in about an hour, after much diving, he auceeerled in finding the liens,, d. and brought him to the side. I took him from bin]. 1 here were many people there. He was not dead when in came up out of the water. We turned hint upaide down, and allowed wafer to run from hitn. He lived about five nrinut s alter he got to hie lodgings. He never spoke, and took no notice of what wee going on. I. with others; took him tome. The other man came out of the water and began crying.—Jolin QA/111, re- siding in Taylor's-row, Sutton, toil I was passing over the railway bridge with Edward Littler, when I heard some- one tray that a man was drowning. We ran to the place,and I undreemd myself, and divell in to me ill could find the deceased. I could not, find him the first time, and eo I dived down a second time, and touched him. Ile wan alive then, I believe, for bit arm was in motion. I got hold of him, but I was very much exhausted and wae obliged to open my mouth, thereby taking no large quantity of water. I let co and went to the surface, where I gave up the water Iliad ewallowed. I divt.l down again as I knew lie war alive. and I was anxious to save his life if possible. I touched the bottom with my head, and got hold of sleerased and brought him to the surface.—The coroner thought it was a piece of fool- hardiness on the part of the men to go and have a swim in that canal. They were both forwaid in drink according to the witnesses.—The coroner and the jury complimented John Quinn on his noble conduct, and raid that be bad acted inn prompt aild gallant manner. 000 01 the jurors asked if nothing could be given to Quinn as a testimony for his services—The coroner said that only certainsocietien did that, unless a numbg of gentlemen opened a subscrip- tion on his behalf. A swimmer, however, had a privifige which no other man poseessell, and tbe fact that a man could en-ins ought to be looked upon sea privilege held. At the Runcorn Police Court ori Monday, before the Rev. B. A. P. Canipbell and Mr. H. Reynolds. Mr. Joseph Williams, gentleman, of Irwelldane, who has for a great number of years been a member of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, was charged with having on the 10th April, in the township of Runcorn, pending the election of guardians of the poor for the said township, under the s'atutes in that hchalf, wilfully fraudulently, end with intent to affect the rmult of the said election, unlawfully altered or defaced the voting paper of one Ann Evans, and of one Welter Hough, used in the said election. Mr W. H. Linaker appeared on behalf of Mr. H. Linaker, clerk to the Runcorn Board of Guardians. Mr. Graham (front the office of Messrs. ktobert Boris and Co., Warrington) defended. There was a large attendance of the piddle. Anionget the spectators were Mr. Philip Speakman. Mn. Thomas Gregson, Mr. Charles Houghton, and Mr. John Lee. Mr. Williams was accommodated with a seat next to Mr. Graham at the solicitors' table. . .

The summons in the sue of the man Hough was first read over by Mr. Ashton, magistrates clerk. Mr. Graham asked why the c Ise of Evans could not be taken first, on the ground that this was the surnnsons melt with on the previous hearing. Mr. Linakes It does not matter. Mr. Grab... They will all have to be over into. After souse discussion.

'Ube Chairman said : As this case of Evans has already been partly heard, we may as well go on with it. Mr. ',looker: I hare no objections, Mr Graham: I should like, in the first place, to see the information and the authmity to prosecute. Mr. Henry Linaker odd he hail not got with Wen any authority to prosecute. Mr. Linaker (to the Chairman). The clerk to the Guar- dians must institute the prosecution, sir. Mr. Graham: I wish you would point that out to me. The Chairman : Is there any dispute about the charge! Mr. Linaker This objection was not taken when the case came on before. Mr. Graham : I never opened my ease on that 0.291011. . .
Mr. Linaket The returning officer I. the pnmecutor, and he will himself prove that he is acting under the authority of Ids Beard. . .
Thp Chairman: If the retuning officer is the prosecutor, I should prefer that he should have hie way. What does 1,, wish ? '

Me Graham: We must follow the statute, .your worship, whatever the returning officer may wish. It Is provided by :astute that the authority shall have the print and the seal of the Chairman of tho Hoard of Guardians, and I call for that authority. The Chairman: Are you authorized to to sot Mr. Henry Limber : I have been authorized by the Board of Civardians to prosecute in this case, but I have not the minute book here.

PRODSHAM PARISH Curnen.—Oa Sunday last, the special aervice for the 20th of June, being the anniversary of the day on which Her Majesty began her happy reign, was used at thi. church. A sermon, crpropor, of the occasion was preached by the Rev. Alfred P. Reynolds, curate, And at the close the organ pealed forth the inspiriting tones of the National Anthem. Sunday nest will be the last day on . which service will be held prior to the thorough restoration

CRICKFT Ctrs —A cricket club for Frodsham is again under consideration, and a meeting to arrange details and settle rules has been convened for this day. There is some talk of a field being obtained and laid down for recreation such as cricket and football, for those who are disposed for active exereirr, and lawn tennis he., as a milder form of amusement. We heartily wish the movement success, and if the same promote s will give their attention to pro- viding a reading room for winter evening recreation, it will be another step to the development of social life in frodsharn.
